label: Orthogonal Association
notes: We open the chapter by framing the central question: when two orientations are observed together, how do we model and measure the way one predicts the other. Throughout, frames live on Stiefel manifolds, and association is read off the geometry that couples them.

label: Paired Frames on Stiefel Manifolds
notes: Each observation is now a pair of orthonormal frames rather than a single one. We fix notation for the two Stiefel manifolds, recall that columns are orthonormal, and stress that the sample is a list of coupled frames whose joint distribution carries all dependence information.

label: The Cross-Product Matrix
notes: The transpose product of two paired frames is the chapter workhorse. It collapses each pair into a compact matrix whose singular values summarise alignment. We interpret large singular values as strong directional agreement and a vanishing average as the signature of independence between frames.

label: Independent versus Associated
notes: Two contrasting pictures anchor intuition. Under independence the second frame is uniformly random given the first, so relative orientations scatter uniformly. Under strong association the second frame clusters near a fixed rotation of the first, and the resultant cross-product matrix grows away from zero.

label: Joint Matrix-Langevin Model
notes: We build a joint density coupling the two frames through a bilinear exponent. The coupling matrix plays the role of a directional regression coefficient: setting it to zero factorises the density into independent marginals, while a large coupling concentrates the conditional orientation of one frame around the other.

label: Conditional Orientation
notes: Conditioning one frame on the other yields again a matrix-Langevin law, now centred at a rotated copy of the conditioning frame. This conditional view turns the coupling matrix into a predictor of orientation and explains why the model behaves like directional regression between frames.

label: Measures of Association
notes: We define scalar summaries of dependence built from the mean cross-product matrix. Its singular values, suitably normalised, give canonical association coefficients lying between zero and one, with zero meaning no association and one meaning a deterministic orthogonal relationship between the two frames.

label: Canonical Correlation of Frames
notes: Singular vectors of the mean cross-product matrix pick out paired directions that are maximally associated, exactly mirroring classical canonical correlation analysis. Each singular value is a canonical correlation between a direction in one frame and a matched direction in the other frame.

label: Estimating the Coupling
notes: Given a sample of paired frames we average the cross-product matrices and take its singular value decomposition. The orthogonal factors estimate the alignment rotations and the singular values estimate the canonical association coefficients, giving a complete moment-style fit of the coupling structure.

label: Testing Independence
notes: Independence corresponds to a zero coupling matrix, so its sample analogue tests the hypothesis directly. We form a statistic from the summed squared singular values of the mean cross-product matrix, whose null distribution is approximately chi-squared by a standard large-sample expansion.

label: Worked Diagnostic
notes: We trace a small numerical pipeline: simulate paired frames, average their cross-products, decompose, and read the resultant norm as a diagnostic. Watching that diagnostic rise as the coupling strengthens confirms that the measure tracks association exactly as the theory predicts it should.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We close by collecting the chapter's invariants: the cross-product matrix, its singular values as canonical correlations, and the independence test built from them. These tools generalise correlation to orientation data and set up the inference machinery used in later chapters on directional regression.
